column2: Which governance decisions belong at enterprise rather than individual repository scope?
column3: Organisation-wide mandatory boundaries, while repository-specific ownership and implementation settings remain delegated where allowed.

column2: What bottleneck can centralised governance create?
column3: A central team may become the approval or implementation queue for every change unless it provides clear delegated controls.

column2: What should accompany delegated repository administration?
column3: Explicit authority limits, an accountable owner and monitoring of changes and exceptions.

column2: Can a lower GitHub scope always relax an enterprise-enforced Actions restriction?
column3: No. Lower scopes remain constrained by applicable enterprise policies.

column2: What makes a repository baseline measurable?
column3: Concrete requirements such as named ownership, restricted access, required reviews and passing checks, each with inspectable state.

column2: Who should own repository access review and retirement decisions?
column3: A named accountable service or repository owner, with supporting administration responsibilities documented.

column2: What stages should a governance exception pass through?
column3: Request with rationale, risk-owner approval, time-bounded application, review and removal or explicit renewal.

column2: When should a GitHub Actions restriction be enforced at enterprise scope?
column3: When it must apply consistently across all governed organisations and local administrators must not relax it.

column2: Which GitHub ruleset controls express reviewed and validated changes to main?
column3: Require pull requests and appropriate reviews and status checks, with carefully limited bypass actors.

column2: Which policies constrain what GitHub automation may execute?
column3: Enablement rules and allowed actions/reusable workflows, supported pinning restrictions and token permission settings.

column2: Is distributing a GitHub workflow file enough to require its successful validation?
column3: No. Use supported required status checks or required-workflow rules, checking plan, repository eligibility and bypass configuration.

column2: What should a third-party action approval policy assess?
column3: Publisher and code provenance, revision pinning, transitive dependencies, requested privileges and update ownership.

column2: Why do approved GitHub workflow templates need ongoing enforcement?
column3: Copies can drift or be edited; enforce required outcomes and manage updates to shared logic.

column2: How can GitHub repository custom properties support governance?
column3: Classify repositories by attributes such as sensitivity or service ownership for inventory and supported policy targeting.

column2: Which audit evidence helps investigate a GitHub organisation policy change?
column3: Actor, action, time and affected organisation or repository, correlated with resulting configuration and runs.

column2: What should a GitHub App governance process cover?
column3: Accountable ownership, approved installations and permissions, secret/key handling, periodic review and removal when retired.

column2: Why avoid granting Azure organisation administration for a project-only duty?
column3: It gives authority beyond the required project scope and increases the impact of mistakes or compromise.

column2: Does an Azure project-scoped build identity make every cross-project operation impossible?
column3: No. Explicit resource permissions can authorise required access; project scope narrows the default identity boundary.

column2: Which Azure branch controls enforce review and validation before integration?
column3: Blocking reviewer and build-validation policies on the protected target branch, with bypass permissions constrained.

column2: How can an Azure extends template restrict consumers?
column3: It defines the outer pipeline and permitted parameters or steps, limiting what consumers can insert.

column2: Which production resource is a useful place for an Azure required-template check?
column3: The production service connection or another supported protected resource whose consumers must use the approved template.

column2: What controls should protect a production Azure service connection?
column3: Selected pipeline authorisation, limited administrators, minimum Azure permissions and suitable approvals or checks.

column2: What must be checked before a project uses a sensitive Azure agent pool?
column3: Project queue/pool rights, pipeline authorisation and any checks, together with the workload's trust level.

column2: Why separate pipeline-edit permission from protected-resource administration?
column3: An editor should not be able to silently grant their own modified pipeline production authority.
